title: Summit Climbing Gym: first payroll, employee deductions, employer payroll taxes and remittances
participant_role: Payroll accountant at an accounting firm helping a new client run its first payroll
judge_role: Owner of Summit Climbing Gym, who just hired three hourly employees and wants to "just pay them what they earned"

difficulty.rationale: Payroll with overtime, withholdings, employer taxes and two entries.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a payroll accountant at an accounting firm. The owner (judge) of SUMMIT CLIMBING GYM, a new client, wants you to help run the gym's first payroll.

SUMMIT CLIMBING GYM opened three months ago. Until now, the owner (judge) did all of the work alone. Last week the owner (judge) hired the gym's first three hourly employees: a route setter, a front desk associate and a climbing instructor. The owner (judge) plans to "just pay them what they earned" by writing each employee a check for hours worked times the hourly rate. The owner (judge) does not understand why anything should be taken out of the checks or why the gym would owe anything more than the wages.

The gym pays employees weekly. Overtime is paid at 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a week. The timecards and the federal income tax withholding amounts (taken from the IRS withholding tables using each employee's Form W-4) are shown below.

[Weekly timecards: see exhibits]

[Payroll tax rates: see exhibits]

The owner (judge) wants to know exactly how much each employee takes home, what this payroll really costs the gym, how to record it in the books and what the gym must send to the government.

You must:
- Calculate each employee's gross earnings
- Calculate the employee deductions and Alex's net pay
- Calculate the employer's payroll taxes
- Journalize the payroll and the employer's payroll tax expense
- Explain what must be deposited and filed, and when

You will present the information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's (judge's) office at the gym. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Could I just call them independent contractors and skip all of this?
Brooke asked what Alex makes. Can I tell her?

solution.overview: A strong answer computes gross pay of $2,000 (including Alex's $150 of overtime), shows that employees take home $1,617 after $383 of withholdings and that the gym also owes $225 of employer taxes, for a total payroll cost of $2,225. The presenter then journalizes both payroll entries and explains the deposit and filing calendar (EFTPS, Form 941, Form 940, state returns, W-2s).

answer: Alex: 40 hours x $20 = $800 regular plus 5 overtime hours x $30 = $150, so $950
Overtime rate = $20 x 1.5 = $30 per hour
Brooke: 35 x $18 = $630 (no overtime)
Carlos: 30 x $14 = $420 (no overtime)
Total gross payroll = $2,000

by_task.task: Employee deductions and Alex's net pay
answer: Social Security 6.2% x 2,000 = $124; Medicare 1.45% x 2,000 = $29
Federal income tax 95 + 50 + 25 = $170; state income tax 3% x 2,000 = $60
Total deductions $383, so total net pay = 2,000 minus 383 = $1,617
Alex: 950 minus 58.90 SS minus 13.78 Medicare minus 95.00 FIT minus 28.50 SIT = $753.82
These amounts belong to the government; the gym only holds them until it pays them
Employer matches Social Security $124 and Medicare $29
Total employer payroll taxes = $225
True cost of this payroll to the gym = 2,000 + 225 = $2,225, not $2,000
Entry 1 records gross wages as Wages Expense and each withholding as a liability
Net pay of $1,617 is credited to Wages Payable (or Cash if paid the same day)
Entry 2 records the employer's taxes as Payroll Tax Expense with a liability for each tax
Each entry balances: $2,000 in entry 1 and $225 in entry 2
Deposit federal income tax withheld plus both halves of Social Security and Medicare electronically through EFTPS on the monthly or semiweekly schedule
File Form 941 every quarter to report wages, withholding and FICA
File Form 940 annually for FUTA; deposit FUTA only when the liability exceeds $500
Pay SUTA and state income tax withholding to the state on its schedule
Give W-2s to employees and file them with the SSA by January 31; keep timecards and earnings records

calculations.label: Total employee deductions and net pay
Employer payroll taxes and total cost

judge_question_answers.question: Could I just call them independent contractors and skip all of this?
answer: No: classification depends on control, not on the label you choose
You set their schedules, train them and provide the equipment, so they are employees
Misclassification can bring back payroll taxes, interest and penalties from the IRS and the state
Employees also lose unemployment and workers' compensation protection

judge_question_answers.question: Brooke asked what Alex makes. Can I tell her?
answer: Payroll records are confidential, so you should not share one employee's pay with another
Protect records with limited access (locked files, passwords)
Employees may choose to discuss their own pay, but the owner should not disclose it for them
Explain that pay reflects the role: route setting is a different job with different skills

key_concepts.definition: Total pay before any deductions. Gross = regular hours x rate + overtime hours x overtime rate.
Extra pay for hours over 40 in a workweek for hourly employees. Overtime rate = regular rate x 1.5.
The take-home amount on the paycheck. Net pay = gross earnings minus all deductions.
Federal taxes that fund retirement and health programs. The employee pays 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare, and the employer matches both.
Federal and state income tax taken out of each paycheck and sent to the government for the employee. The federal amount comes from IRS tables using the employee's Form W-4.
Federal and state unemployment taxes paid only by the employer. They are charged on each employee's wages up to a yearly wage base ($7,000 for FUTA).
The employer's own cost of payroll taxes (its share of FICA plus FUTA and SUTA), recorded separately from wages expense.
Amounts withheld or owed that the business must later pay to the government or employees, such as Social Security Tax Payable and Wages Payable.
EFTPS is the electronic system for depositing federal payroll taxes. Form 941 is the quarterly return that reports wages, withholding and FICA.
Form 940 is the annual FUTA return. Form W-2 reports each employee's yearly wages and withholding and is due to employees and the SSA by January 31.
A worker is an employee when the business controls how, when and where the work is done. Employers must withhold and pay payroll taxes for employees but not for true contractors.

notes: State level because students must handle overtime, both employee and employer taxes, two multi-line journal entries and the full remittance calendar in 10 minutes. Watch for students who forget the overtime premium, who deduct employer taxes from employee pay, or who treat the employer's FICA match as a withholding instead of an expense.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates Alex's pay as $800 regular plus 5 overtime hours at $30 ($150) for $950, Brooke $630 and Carlos $420, for total gross payroll of $2,000, and explains the 1.5 times overtime rule for hours over 40.
criteria.meets: Calculates gross earnings of $950, $630 and $420 for a total of $2,000, including Alex's overtime.
criteria.below: Gets most earnings right but misses the overtime premium (paying Alex $900) or makes an arithmetic error in the total.
criteria.little: Does not calculate gross earnings, or the numbers are unrelated to the timecards.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates Social Security $124, Medicare $29, federal income tax $170 and state income tax $60 for $383 of deductions and $1,617 of net pay, works out Alex's net pay of $753.82, and explains that withholdings belong to the government and the gym only holds them.
criteria.meets: Calculates total deductions of $383, total net pay of $1,617 and Alex's net pay of $753.82.
criteria.below: Leaves out one deduction, uses the wrong rate, or deducts employer taxes (such as FUTA or SUTA) from employee pay.
criteria.little: Does not calculate deductions, or agrees to pay employees their full gross pay.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates the employer's Social Security match $124, Medicare match $29, FUTA $12 and SUTA $60 for $225 of employer taxes, and shows the owner that the true payroll cost is $2,225, not $2,000.
criteria.meets: Calculates employer payroll taxes of $225 and a total payroll cost of $2,225.
criteria.below: Leaves out the employer's FICA match or one of the unemployment taxes, or gives a wrong total.
criteria.little: Does not calculate employer taxes, or says the gym owes nothing beyond wages.

criteria.exceeds: Records entry 1 (debit Wages Expense $2,000; credit Social Security Tax Payable $124, Medicare Tax Payable $29, Federal Income Tax Payable $170, State Income Tax Payable $60, Wages Payable $1,617) and entry 2 (debit Payroll Tax Expense $225; credit Social Security $124, Medicare $29, FUTA $12, SUTA $60 payables), and explains that each balances.
criteria.meets: Records both entries with the correct accounts and amounts, $2,000 in entry 1 and $225 in entry 2.
criteria.below: Records only one entry, combines them incorrectly, or treats the employer's FICA match as a withholding from employees.
criteria.little: Gives no journal entries, or entries with unrelated accounts.

criteria.exceeds: Explains depositing federal income tax plus both halves of Social Security and Medicare through EFTPS on the monthly or semiweekly schedule, quarterly Form 941, annual Form 940 (FUTA deposited only above $500), state SUTA and withholding payments, and W-2s by January 31, plus keeping timecards and earnings records.
criteria.meets: Explains EFTPS deposits, Form 941 quarterly, Form 940 annually, state payments and W-2s by January 31.
criteria.below: Mentions paying the government but leaves out key forms or deadlines.
criteria.little: Does not explain deposits or filings.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects gross pay, withholdings, employer taxes, journal entries and remittances into one flow and shows why the gym's cost is $2,225 while employees take home $1,617.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the timecards and rates to gross pay, deductions and employer taxes.
criteria.below: Reaches conclusions without showing the reasoning, or confuses employee and employer taxes.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Corrects the owner's plan to "just pay them what they earned" and gives a practical plan: budget $2,225 a week, set up EFTPS and follow the filing calendar.
criteria.meets: Clearly explains why the owner cannot pay gross wages and what the gym must do instead.
criteria.below: Identifies the problem but gives an incomplete plan.
criteria.little: Offers no solution to the owner's payroll problem.

criteria.exceeds: Explains payroll terms in plain language a first-time employer can follow, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents earnings, deductions, taxes, entries and filings clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a payroll register or a simple breakdown ($2,000 gross, $383 withheld, $1,617 take-home, $225 employer taxes, $2,225 cost) and a filing calendar that makes the owner's duties easy to follow.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the payroll easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: classification depends on control, and because the owner sets schedules, trains and provides equipment they are employees, with back taxes, interest and penalties for misclassification; and payroll records are confidential, so the owner should not share Alex's pay with Brooke and should limit access to records.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that the workers are employees and that one employee's pay should not be shared with another.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without reasons.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or agrees to call the workers independent contractors.

key_points: Gross pay: Alex $950 ($800 regular plus $150 overtime at $30), Brooke $630, Carlos $420, total $2,000
Employee deductions: Social Security $124, Medicare $29, federal income tax $170, state income tax $60, total $383; net pay $1,617
Employer taxes: Social Security $124, Medicare $29, FUTA $12, SUTA $60, total $225; true payroll cost $2,225
Entry 1: debit Wages Expense $2,000; credit the four withholding payables and Wages Payable $1,617
Entry 2: debit Payroll Tax Expense $225; credit Social Security, Medicare, FUTA and SUTA payables
Deposit through EFTPS; file Form 941 quarterly and Form 940 annually; pay state taxes; give W-2s by January 31
The workers are employees, not independent contractors, and payroll records are confidential
